analysis.one_liner: Bans a list of toxic chemicals, including PFAS and phthalates, from food packaging.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 15 House sponsors in June 2026, has sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee with no hearing, markup, or vote ever scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite federal food-additive law to declare a specific list of chemicals unsafe for any use in materials that touch food. The list includes PFAS ("forever chemicals"), ortho-phthalates, bisphenols (including BPA), and industrial chemicals like formaldehyde, benzene, and asbestos. It would take effect two years after enactment, require regulators to weigh effects on children, pregnant women, and other vulnerable groups when evaluating replacement chemicals, and explicitly preserve the right of states and cities to pass stricter rules of their own.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats packaged or processed food — effectively the whole public — would get lower exposure to chemicals linked in the scientific record to hormone disruption, developmental harm, and cancer risk. Children, pregnant women, and workers in food packaging plants would benefit most, since the bill requires special attention to disproportionately exposed groups. Companies making safer packaging alternatives would also gain a market as the banned chemicals are phased out.

how_it_helps.text: Deems 15 classes or specific chemicals unsafe as food contact substances — including PFAS, ortho-phthalates, bisphenols (BPA, BPS, BPF), styrene polymers, formaldehyde, benzene, and asbestos — removing them from materials that touch food.

Requires the Food and Drug Administration to consider potential harm to vulnerable populations — infants, children, pregnant women, the elderly, workers, and overexposed communities — when judging safety of any substitute chemical.
Preserves the power of states and cities to enact stricter food-packaging rules than the federal floor, preventing a national standard from overriding tougher local protections.
Gives manufacturers a two-year runway after enactment to reformulate packaging before the ban takes effect.

analysis.who_pays: Food packaging manufacturers and the chemical companies that supply them would bear reformulation costs, replacing PFAS grease-proofing, phthalate plasticizers, and bisphenol-based coatings with safer alternatives. Food brands could face higher packaging input costs, some portion of which may reach consumers as prices. Regulators at FDA would take on new petition-review work.

drawbacks.text: A blanket ban on entire chemical classes, rather than case-by-case safety limits, could force rapid substitution with alternatives whose own safety is not yet established — which is why the bill requires regulators to scrutinize replacement chemicals for vulnerable populations.
Reformulating packaging and supply chains on a two-year timeline could raise costs for food manufacturers, some of which may be passed to consumers as higher prices.

Some listed substances (for example, styrene polymers in common plastics) are used in a very wide range of food-contact materials, so compliance burdens would fall broadly across the packaging industry rather than on a few products.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit — removing a defined list of chemicals with documented links to hormone disruption and cancer risk from food contact — is large and broad-based, and the two-year delay and state-preservation provisions give the rule flexibility. The main honest cost is transition expense for packaging makers and possible price pass-through, plus the risk that some substitutes prove problematic; the bill partially addresses that by requiring scrutiny of alternatives. The bill was not debated, so the objections above were never tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and has had no hearing, markup, or floor action since.

narrative.text: Representative Janice Schakowsky introduced the No Toxic Chemicals in Food Packaging Act of 2026 on June 9, 2026, with 10 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day it was introduced.
Fourteen additional House members signed on as cosponsors, all Democrats; no Republican cosponsor joined.
After referral, the bill has taken no further action — no committee report, hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in its action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of PFAS-treated, phthalate-plasticized, and bisphenol-based food packaging keep selling products that would otherwise be phased out within two years, because no committee or floor vote has moved the bill toward law. Consumers continue to be exposed to the listed chemicals in food packaging.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Packaging and chemical makers; the bill went nowhere

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban 15 listed toxic chemicals from food packaging and recruited 14 cosponsors.

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro and 13 other House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original or added cosponsors; all 14 were Democrats, none Republican.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or report — leaving it without a path to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 supporters in the House were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-led committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: Would have to strip PFAS grease-proofing, phthalate plasticizers, and bisphenol coatings from products that touch food within two years. Their interest in keeping current cheap materials runs against the public's interest in lower chemical exposure.

industries.industry: Chemical suppliers (PFAS, phthalate, and specialty chemical makers)
industries.note: Would lose a food-contact market for entire chemical classes that the bill deems unsafe. The bill would not restrict these chemicals' non-food uses.
Producers of PFAS-free and phthalate-free packaging would gain demand as brands reformulate. Their gain tracks the public's interest in safer packaging.
Would face reformulation and possible input-cost increases, but would also shed liability and consumer concern tied to the banned chemicals in their packaging.

analysis.trajectory: With a bare-minimum sponsor list of 15 House Democrats, no Republican support, and no committee action months after referral, the bill follows the usual path of single-chamber health-and-safety bills: it is likely to sit in the Energy and Commerce Committee and expire at the end of the 119th Congress in January 2027 without a vote.
